title: Constantine's Ambiguous Legislation on Magic
description: Constantine issued several pieces of legislation on magic in the 310s-320s CE that collectively established an ambiguous framework distinguishing beneficial from harmful magic. A rescript of 318/319 CE exempted haruspices (diviners) from penalties when consulted for legitimate purposes such as lightning strikes, while a law of 321 CE specifically permitted magic used to benefit agriculture or medicine but prohibited that used to harm. This distinction between beneficial and malefic magic would become fundamental to later Christian legal thinking, though Constantine simultaneously issued edicts against nocturnal sacrifices. The legislation reflects a transitional moment between Roman tolerance of certain magical practices and Christian systematization.
historiographical_note: John Curran and Ramsay MacMullen have analyzed Constantine's magic legislation as revealing the complex transitional character of his reign — Christian in identity but pragmatically tolerant of traditional practices — a position that created lasting ambiguity in the legal treatment of magic.
source_method: Published scholarship; Codex Theodosianus 9.16; secondary scholarship on late Roman law
